1.pericope_label: An angel come down from heaven, having the key of the bottomless pit

schools.summary: Gill rules out Constantine and the apostles and sets the scene of a devil left standing alone.
Henry identifies the angel with Christ himself, as the only one strong enough to bind the strong man, and counts the chain and key as two instruments.

Ellicott refuses the identification as needless and locates the power in the one holding the keys of death; Robertson glosses the chain and its position; Barnes maps the chapter and names the enemies already destroyed.
Wesley distinguishes the angel from Christ on the analogy of Michael casting out the dragon; Clarke treats him as an officer of divine justice.
Victorinus of Pettau makes the binding present since the first advent and the abyss the hearts of the wicked; Bede reads the vision as recapitulation and the names of Satan as a character sketch.

debates.question: Who is the angel that binds Satan?

sides.position: Christ himself; no other answers the description
A created angel, as Michael cast the dragon out of heaven
An executor of divine justice, a jailer rather than a person to be named
Neither Constantine nor any apostle, whatever else he may be
The question is needless; the key and chain show whose power is at work

outliers.note: Places the binding in the present age, running from the first advent, and reads the abyss as the hearts of the wicked rather than a place.

2.pericope_label: The dragon seized, bound, and shut in the abyss for a thousand years

schools.summary: Gill denies that the dragon is Paganism and identifies him as the devil himself; he treats the pit as the prison the demons dreaded, distinct from the lake of fire.

Barnes weighs the verb of seizure and infers a superior power; Ellicott reads the four titles as a portrait and calls the date of the binding a needless question; Robertson notes the grammatical break and rests the number on the apostolic saying about a day and a thousand years.

Clarke refuses a literal thousand years and rebukes the recurring expectation of a datable millennium; Wesley argues in five steps that the years wholly follow the beast and are therefore still future.

debates.question: Is the thousand years a literal period?

sides.position: No; the number is symbolic like every other number in the book, and marks a lengthened season
A real era still to come, since the blessings described have never yet been seen

debates.question: Can the moment of the binding be fixed?

sides.position: It is not needful to inquire; what the vision shows as instant may be gradual in fulfilment
No intimation is given, and it is impossible to conjecture
Who can tell in what the binding consists

4.pericope_label: Thrones, judgment given, and the souls of the beheaded living and reigning

schools.summary: Gill has thrones pitched for all the saints, sitting as kings and conquerors in undisturbed peace.
Henry expects a period of universal pure Christianity after the fall of the persecuting powers, wrought by the Spirit.

Barnes refuses to name the occupants and reads the thrones as set for judgment on the pattern of Daniel; Robertson lists the candidates and glosses the axe-word and the ambiguous aorist of living; Ellicott identifies the occupants as all the real servants of God in two classes, martyrs and the faithful in life.

Wesley distinguishes the enthroned from the souls and from the saints already raised, and places the reign in heaven with bodies reunited; Clarke reads the thrones as Christianity established on earth and the martyrs living in the revival of their testimony.

sides.position: Not stated, and not to be supplied; the text names no one
All the real servants of God, martyrs and the faithful in life alike
Perhaps Christ and the apostles, perhaps some of the saints, perhaps the martyrs
In heaven, not on earth; the earthly reign named earlier is another thing
On earth, in a long prosperity where the Gospel so prevails that Christ appears to reign

5.pericope_label: The rest of the dead lived not until the thousand years were finished

schools.summary: Gill restricts the rest of the dead to the wicked, bodily dead, since the saints rise together.

Barnes takes them for the less eminent pious dead and the whole passage as a matter of honour rather than of bodies; Ellicott denies that resurrection must be read literally and shows the figure at work elsewhere in Scripture; Robertson refuses to decide, doubts the genuineness of the closing clause, and sets the general resurrection against a special one.
Clarke calls the common martyr-resurrection view very doubtful; Wesley distinguishes two separate thousand-year periods, both transacted invisibly, to reconcile prophecies that appear to clash.

debates.question: Who are the rest of the dead?

sides.position: The wicked dead only
The pious dead of less eminence, honoured later and less
All except the martyrs, righteous and unrighteous together — though others restrict it to the wicked
Not necessarily; Scripture uses resurrection figuratively of the spiritually dead
The commonly supposed bodily raising of the martyrs is very doubtful
No solid conception is available; the symbolism resists ordinary narrative exegesis

6.pericope_label: Blessed and holy is he that hath part in the first resurrection

schools.summary: Gill reads the clause as either describing who shares the resurrection — only the justified and regenerate — or describing their perfected blessedness and holiness in soul and body.

Robertson numbers the beatitude, leaves the nature of the two resurrections undecided, and notes that the earlier promise of reigning upon earth is absent here; Ellicott makes the second death spiritual and the priesthood and kingship those of a life offered up; Barnes reads the blessing as encouragement to the persecuted and concedes the verse is the mainstay of literal-millennium teaching.
Clarke ties holiness to the trial of martyrdom and traces both the second death and the idiom of having no power to Jewish usage; Wesley infers the deity of Christ from the joint priesthood.

debates.question: Who are the blessed and holy?

sides.position: The martyrs, holy because tried when nothing but holiness was tried
Those justified, pardoned and regenerated, and none besides
All who have offered themselves a living sacrifice and overcome the world-powers

debates.question: Where do the priests and kings reign?

sides.position: No hint is given; the earlier promise of reigning upon earth is not repeated here
With Christ for a thousand years, without further specification

7.pericope_label: Satan loosed, and the nations gathered as Gog and Magog

schools.summary: Gill dates the years as still unexpired and refutes the proposed medieval terminal dates.
Henry treats the loosing as a standing fact of this world and turns it into a rebuke of slack service.

Barnes refuses to explain the release and reduces it to a local outbreak of wickedness; Ellicott reads the millennium as a closing opportunity and the invasion as Christendom overrun; Robertson takes the names figuratively and argues the vast host proves Satan keeps a following throughout.

Clarke argues from the sequence of binding, peace, loosing and war that no literal reading is possible; Wesley keeps Gog and Magog as an actual northern prince and people whose name will be known in the event.

debates.question: Are Gog and Magog actual nations?

sides.position: Figurative; no single nation answers to the nations in the four corners of the earth
A real northern people and their prince, described more fully by the earlier prophet

debates.question: Have the thousand years already run?

sides.position: Not yet; the medieval dates proposed for their close all fail
The question is misconceived, since the whole sequence resists literal reading

9.pericope_label: The camp of the saints compassed, fire from heaven, and the devil cast into the lake

schools.summary: Gill allows the whole earth or the land of Israel, and notes the devil deceives these nations both before death and after their rising.

Barnes reads the invasion as figure for organised hostility and marks the symmetry of the devil sharing the beast’s doom; Ellicott identifies the beloved city with Jerusalem as figure of the faithful Zion and gathers the Old Testament fires behind the flame; Robertson glosses the military vocabulary and reports the division over whether the city is Jerusalem or the Church.

Clarke makes the city Jerusalem primarily and the Church typically, and marks the difference between restrained power and power totally taken away; Wesley locates the camp in the gentile church around Jerusalem and reads the torment as unremitting.

sides.position: Jerusalem, as the psalms name it — though others read it as the Church, the new Zion
Jerusalem primarily, the Christian Church typically
Jerusalem, and in it the figure of the true spiritual Zion
Perhaps the gentile church dwelling round about Jerusalem

11.pericope_label: A great white throne, and the flight of earth and heaven from his face

schools.summary: Gill declines to apply the vision to the Gospel dispensation, though he grants that period its own shaking, its own opened books and its own disclosure of the book of life.
Henry treats the fall of the devil’s kingdom as the proper occasion of the judgment and contrasts the white tribunal with the throne of iniquity.

Barnes glosses great and white as elevated and shining and reads the flight as apparent vanishing; Ellicott makes the colour a token of the judgment’s purity, holds Father and Son together on the throne, and cautions against reading a physical catastrophe out of poetical language; Robertson notes the added epithet, places the Father on the throne with the Son beside him, and cites the non-eternity of matter.
Clarke names the occupant as Jehovah and takes the dissolution literally; Wesley names him as Christ and presses each negative clause to mean that heaven and earth ceased to exist.

debates.question: Who sits upon the great white throne?

sides.position: The Lord Jesus Christ, at his second advent
The indescribable Jehovah
God as throughout the book, which does not exclude the Son who shares the throne
The Almighty Father, with the Son seated beside him and working with him

debates.question: Does the verse describe a physical dissolution of the universe?

sides.position: Yes; heaven and earth wholly ceased to be
The language is poetical; caution forbids asserting a physical catastrophe
They seem to vanish as stars vanish at sunrise

12.pericope_label: The dead standing before the throne, the books opened, and the sea and death surrendering their dead

schools.summary: Gill restricts these dead to the wicked, the righteous having been judged and enthroned a thousand years earlier, and insists the sea is literal.

Barnes takes the dead to be all the dead and makes the verse an argument against any earlier partial resurrection; Robertson notes the anticipation of the general resurrection, treats the books as written evidence vouching for the book of life, and reports the reading of the sea as figure.

Clarke names the two books, traces the imagery to Daniel, and qualifies judgment by works with the proof they give of faith; Wesley includes those changed without dying and describes an assize where the books are not read but simply made visible.

debates.question: Who are the dead that stand before the throne?

sides.position: All the dead, righteous and wicked alike — which rules out an earlier resurrection of part of them
Only the rest of the dead, the wicked; the righteous were judged a thousand years before

debates.question: On what basis is the sentence passed?

sides.position: On works, and on faith also, since the works prove whether the faith was true
Saved by grace, but character at last is the test, as the fruit is of the tree
On the recorded deeds, exhibited as evidence is exhibited in a court

14.pericope_label: Death and hades cast into the lake of fire, which is the second death

schools.summary: Gill objects that hell cannot be cast into hell and canvasses the alternatives, settling on the wicked dead delivered up and sentenced; he names those the book will not contain.

Barnes reads the verse as the destruction of the last enemy and argues from the surviving second death that universal salvation cannot be meant; Robertson turns the note into a song of victory and rules out soul sleeping, an intermediate state, a second chance and annihilation.

Clarke distinguishes the two deaths by their permanence and explains the book of life from the civic register, ending in direct address to the reader; Wesley states the abolition of death and hades in a sentence.

debates.question: What is cast into the lake when death and hades are cast in?

sides.position: Not hell itself, which is the lake; rather the wicked dead they surrendered
Death as the separation of soul and body, abolished so that neither righteous nor wicked die again

debates.question: What does the second death exclude?

sides.position: Universal salvation, since a second death is described as still existing
Soul sleeping, an intermediate state, a second chance, and annihilation
Any recovery whatever; the first death admits a resurrection, this one does not
